maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext: I would have directed this question to the Prime Minister yesterday had he been here at the opening of the sitting. In view of the fact that the decisions which are made will of necessity be ultimately decisions by parliament, the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference are of great concern to parliament. Can the Prime Minister make any report to the house which would enlighten us beyond the statement given following the closed session succeeding the open session on the first day? I would suggest that review of the basis upon which the government hopes to proceed in certain respects would be helpful to all of us in considering what may be done in connection with this matter and any discussion which should take place.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I would not like to go beyond the terms of the communique which we discussed at considerable length, Mr. Speaker, and about which it was frequently commented that since we had proceeded in camera the discussions should not be reported. It is not that I wish to withhold from parliament any information. The communique indicates that there was a discussion of-I will not say "offer" or "proposal" of the federal government because those words were objected to by others attending on the ground that there was nothing complete that could be regarded as an "offer" or as a "proposal"-a suggestion that I put before the meeting on the first day when it was an open public meeting.
It was quite evident, and no one questioned it, that we did not have accurate information that would permit of the establishment of an exact formula. It was decided an endeavour would be made, in the most expeditious manner, to secure that information. It was for that reason a committee was suggested to be made up of the representatives-I do not know that they are all of welfare departments-but on behalf of the welfare department of each of the provinces and
Inquiries of the Ministry representatives of the federal government, to review all the data available and try to get the basis for a formula. It was felt the committee should endeavour to do that with such expedition as would not delay a decision upon it until the October meeting.
The committee would proceed at once, and I understand that they had a preliminary meeting yesterday morning. It was hoped that they might have made sufficient progress to make it practicable to have a meeting of the ministers undertake a study as early as possible-one suggestion had been as early as possible in June and others preferred that the words "in June" be left out. I just mention that as indicating what was meant approximately by "as early as possible". The suggestion was that it might be appropriate to have action taken by legislative bodies, so that if some kind of arrangement were worked out there would be nothing to prevent its being implemented from the early fall onward. I do not know that there is anything more that I can say, without violating the letter, if not the real spirit of the various statements that were made-that we had proceeded in camera, and that our discussions should conserve that character.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Without in any way suggesting that there would be any breach of the confidential character of the discussions, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. In view of the fact that the government has withdrawn its position from that which it stated it was prepared to take in 1945 in regard to the unemployed, I would like to ask the Prime Minister if there are any other specific proposals in the 1945 proposals not yet dealt with from which the government has withdrawn its support. I ask this question because I think it would be helpful in avoiding any unnecessary discussion if there are any other similar cases where the government has withdrawn from the position it took at that time.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I cannot accept the word "withdrawn". There were proposals made as over-all proposals in 1945. They were not accepted. I stated at the opening meeting of this preliminary conference that we did not consider that the proposals that had been made and were not accepted at that time were a proper basis for an agenda of discussions at this time.
There have been a great many things done, not because they were in the proposals but because they were considered to be the right things to do-things done since 1945. But the government does not consider that it is bound in any way by unaccepted proposals that were made in 1945.

speechtext: I think so, because I think they are all concerned-of course there is a varying degree of the importance that has to attach, because of the size of the population, to the views of the people of Ontario and the views of the people of Prince Edward Island, for instance. But it must not be forgotten-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext: Is that an interpretation of the green book and, if it is not, what is it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext:
No, it is not an interpretation of the green book. It is a statement of facts which are real and which have their bearing upon the fiscal relationship between the federal government and the provincial governments. And I think it should not be overlooked that the federal government has no funds of its own. The federal government


has funds that are raised from the people of Canada; and when one speaks of what the federal government should do one is speaking of what should be done on behalf of all of the people of Canada, for one or more parts of the people of Canada; there are not at the present time before the provincial governments, for acceptance or for refusal, the proposals that had been made in 1945.
And I will be perfectly open and frank that, had those proposals been accepted, the federal government, as representing all the people of Canada, would find it at the present time pretty embarrassing to carry out the commitments that would have resulted. Because at that time those proposals were based upon the assumption that $250 million per annum being raised from the people of Canada would be quite sufficient for the defence expenditures of this country. And at the present time the members of this government and, I am sure, a large proportion of the Canadian people, recognize as having the highest priority of all, the expenditures that have to be properly made to do our share of the building up of the defence forces that are apt to be sufficient to deter aggression.
That being the case, I doubt if there are very many in Canada who would feel that it would be proper for the government of Canada to raise more money than is now being raised by increasing taxes.
Now, there may be the suggestion that there could be economies. We are endeavouring to practise economies; but they would be a very small proportion of the total budget that has to be met-not out of the moneys of the government of Canada but out of the moneys raised from the people of Canada generally. And that being the case, there has to be an order of priorities established in respect of the purposes to which the moneys provided annually by the people of Canada can be applied.
It will be suggested that there might be capital investments that could be made without being raised out of the year's current revenues. And that may be possible; but that could only be for such capital investments as would ultimately bring to the Canadian economy more than it would be presently taking out of the Canadian economy.
That is the situation that we have to face, and we might as well be realistic about it. We were perhaps overoptimistic about what could be done in 1945. At the present time-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext:

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question without reference to anything that has been said. In connection with the plan for unemployment that was submitted to the dominion-provincial conference as representing the point of view of the government of Canada, will that plan not come into effect unless accepted by all the provinces, or may it be accepted by one or two provinces and not by the others?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE
speechtext: Well, there has been no consideration given to the matter of whether it would be accepted by one or two and not by the others. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF BASIS OF PROCEDURE

Mr. Chairman, as the minister has said, the estimates of this department were the first to be referred to the new committee on estimates which was set up during this session. It is my expectation, and it will probably be found, that the very extensive consideration given to the estimates there will result in the saving of time in the committee of supply. However, I would not be prepared to go quite so far as the minister has indicated he would wish to see done in

each case; that is, that where a question is raised here which was discussed in that committee, the matter might be left, so far as he is concerned, by merely referring us to the page number at which the discussion in the committee will be found. That the report be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"Your committee has devoted a good deal of attention to the administrative practices of this department, particularly of the immigration branch, with a view to determining whether greater efficiency, and therefore economy, could be effected. Departmental officials laid considerable emphasis on the complicated and time-consuming process involved in, and the very large volume of correspondence necessitated by, the present method of dealing with rejected applications for admission to Canada.
The evidence of these officials appears to establish that the present method necessarily involved great


expense not only to the department but to the applicant and his sponsor in Canada. Cases seem to be decided without reference to the decisions in other cases, and no sufficient attempt seems to be made to establish uniformity of decision. The reference here and in succeeding paragraphs is specifically to cases where a prospective immigrant is sponsored by an applicant who is a Canadian citizen.
It occurs to your committee therefore that it would be desirable, and more economical, if in these cases some more simple method could be devised, whereby reviews might be conducted in accordance with well established and generally understood rules, capable of general application to broad classifications of cases, instead of on the basis of individual discretion of junior officials which is frequently exercised to opposite effect in similar cases.
Furthermore, your committee was disturbed by the evidence of a substantial number of irregularities on the part of some immigration officers, involving acceptance of secret commissions or bribes. Evidence was given-
I want to stress that this was evidence that was given before the committee.
-that there were four groups of such cases arising out of applications processed through the Montreal office alone, the fourth group involving a minimum of 75 individual applications. The effect of the bribes was either to secure improper advancement of applications or in some cases the illegal admission of applicants. Your committee appreciates that loyal service is given by the vast majority of immigration officials, but cannot overlook the urgency of ensuring that administrative procedures be reviewed to ensure the elimination of such incidents in future.
In this respect, the secrecy which surrounds the processing of immigration applications, and the lack of opportunities to the applicant, his sponsor, or their solicitor, to inspect files and obtain full information as to the reasons for the disposition of the case, coupled with the enormously wide discretionary power given to immigration officers under the act, do seem to your committee to bring about a set of circumstances where these officers are placed in a position which invites the unscrupulous to take advantage of opportunities for improper personal profit with very little chance of detection.
Your committee desires to emphasize its admiration and respect for the loyalty of all but a small fraction of the officers, but feels that in fairness to the great body of honest officials, as well as from the point of view of increased economy and efficiency, every precaution should be taken to ensure that dishonesty cannot be practised by the few with impunity.
It became apparent also in the course of the committee's study that the present practice results in a refusal of information and reasons to applicants and their sponsors who are Canadian citizens, which is quite contrary to generally accepted concepts of what should be expected from an administrative body, and produces a deep sense of injustice.
All the foregoing considerations have led your committee to conclude that the setting up of a simple and routine review procedure for rejected cases, in which the maximum amount of information consistent with security would be furnished as to the reasons for rejection, would result in a very substantial saving of time and money to the department and to the applicant and his Canadian sponsor, would minimize the chances for corrupt practices, and would bring the administrative practices of the department into conformity with proper standards of justice.

Your committee therefore recommends:
(a)	That the department set up a review board along the lines of the immigration appeal board contemplated in the act.
(b)	That the maximum information consistent with security be furnished to applicants as to reasons for their rejection, and, with the consent of the applicant, be furnished to their Canadian sponsors.
(c)	That the review board give reasons for its decisions and that a body of administrative precedents be thus built up which is available to and known by departmental officials, applicants, sponsors, and their solicitors or counsel.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, I have to point out that that recommendation which we made was rejected by the government majority, in that matter receiving as usual a lead from the minister, although the recommendation was supported, as I recall, by the combined opposition members present at the committee meeting. The Samejima case went from the supreme court of British Columbia to the appeal court of British Columbia to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Brent case has been dragged through the courts and is now apparently going to the topmost rung of the ladder. I submit with greatest respect to Your Honour than the hon. gentleman who has the floor is entitled to refer to a judgment which, until it is appealed, is the final judgment on this matter. This judgment represents an appeal from the original hearing of an application for habeas corpus and a motion by way of certiorari, and it is the final judgment on the subject until another appeal is made. The matter, therefore, is not sub judice, so I would urge with great respect that the hon. gentleman is entitled to proceed.

maintopic: HARBOURS
speechtext: My thought on the point of order was simply this. My understanding of the rule is that it is very clear. A case to be sub judice in the sense that it would be improper to discuss it here has to be before the courts, meaning that either a writ has been issued or some proceedings have been taken to commence action or, in the case of an appeal, that notice of the appeal has been filed. I am reasonably satisfied Your Honour will find that to be the rule; and viewed in that light, the mere declaration by a person of an intention to appeal, or a recommendation to the Attorney General that an appeal should be taken, is not, I think, sufficient to bring it within the rule and make the case sub judice.

maintopic: HARBOURS
speechtext:
With all due deference to the various experts, I am of the opinion that so long as the time for an appeal has not run out, the case is still sub judice. It is not a final judgment if the time for appeal in this

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: HARBOURS
speechtext:
If I may put it this way, a point of order depends not only on a matter of law but on matters of fact as well.
I think the committee will agree that a matter is sub judice which is actually before the court, and cannot properly be discussed within this house. The reason for that rule is fairly obvious, that there shall not be pressure of any kind brought from this legislative body upon the judicial branch of the government. So far I think we can agree.
Then, of course, the question we have before us now is, is this case before the courts or not? I am not prepared to go so far as has been suggested and say that as long as the case is capable of being appealed it may not be discussed here. I understood, in the rather rapid debate that has been going on, that a statement had been made that this case is definitely being appealed. I am in the hands of those who know the facts as to the status of this case. If this case is definitely being appealed in my opinion it is not capable of discussion in this house, for exactly the same reason that it would not be capable of discussion if the appeal were actually being argued, namely that knowing the case was going before the courts it would not be right for members of this house to discuss its merits. I think the committee will agree with me on that.
I believe we shall have to accept the word of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who can tell us definitely whether or not this case is being appealed. If it is, I am going to rule that it should not be discussed at the present time. If it may be or may not be, then of course I am not in a position to rule that it should not be discussed, because we do not know that it is going to be appealed. So far as I am concerned the question is one of fact, as to whether or not this case is definitely being appealed. I would presume the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is the only person who could inform us on that point.

maintopic: HARBOURS
speechtext:
I shall assist the committee, if I can. I have refrained from discussing this
[Mr. Crestohl.l

case because, as I said, I intend to recommend to my colleague the Attorney General that the case be appealed. However, I have not yet made that recommendation to him, and I am not going to make his decision for him. Therefore I do not think one can say that the appeal has yet been entered. This is why I took no exception to what was being said about it by the hon. member for Kamloops or the hon. member for Nanaimo.
I think it would be improper for me to discuss the case, because I do intend to recommend appeal and, as I said before, I intend to recommend appeal because I want the final arbiter to say what the law is. But I would certainly say it is quite proper for the hon. member for Nanaimo to give reasons why he thinks it would be a waste of public money, as he has said, to make the appeal. I should think the hon. member could draw analogies between this and other cases, and so on. I felt I could take no exception to that and, therefore, did not raise the point. My only feeling is that I should not discuss it; but I did not feel that that self-denying ordinance should be applied to any other member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

However, I hope hon. members will agree that perhaps the time has not been wasted. I would hope also that the hon. member for Nanaimo would agree that it is very desirable that in this body we should not at any time discuss the merits of matters which are to be decided by the non-political branch of government, namely the judicial body.
I find myself now in the position that we will have to rely entirely upon the good judgment of the hon. member for Nanaimo as to the language in which he chooses to couch his criticisms of the administration of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Perhaps he would permit me to say, not in any debating sense at all, that in my opinion it would be advisable to be somewhat restrained in any language we might use respecting the merits of a case which we have some reason to believe is due to appear before the final court of appeal in the land.
Further than that I cannot go at the present time, and the hon. member for Nanaimo will be permitted to continue his

remarks and, of course, will not be penalized, in time, for the time lost because of this interruption.

maintopic: HARBOURS

After all, I would point out that it is a precedent followed by many other departments in carrying out regulative powers conferred upon them by the house.

maintopic: HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief. Let me say at the outset that we in this group attach a great deal of importance to the work of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Perhaps this offers a subject that could be exploited politically, but I do not think any useful purpose can be served by doing so. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 285, respecting the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commissioners.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is not unlike the purpose of the bill passed a few moments ago, which was presented to the house by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets). This bill merely consolidates three existing statutes so that the legislation respecting the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commissioners may be found all in one place.
As I have had occasion to point out earlier this session, this legislation was passed first back in 1912, the original Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act being chapter 55 of the statutes of that year. That original statute was amended by chapter 17 of the statutes of 1938, the main purpose of that amendment being to make it possible for some of the other municipalities in the Winnipeg area to have representation on this board. The other amendment was made this session by chapter 6 of the statutes of 1955. As hon. members will recall, the effect of that amendment was to provide that the quorum for meetings of the board should be a majority rather than the larger number under the formula as it stood in the original act.
The bill now before the house in my name makes absolutely no change in the legislation; it does not change a jot or a tittle; it simply brings the three enactments together in one piece of legislation.
As all of us know, about every 25 years there is what is known as a revision of the statutes of Canada, but it so happens that every time that chore is undertaken there are quite a number of statutes not revised, not consolidated and not brought forward. In some cases the reason is quite clear, in that
29, 1955	3311
Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour the usefulness of the statute has diminished or perhaps a statute is spent. In other cases even though the statute may still be in effect those doing the revising do not bring it forward. That is what happened with respect to the Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour Commissioners Act.
There have been two revisions of the statutes since 1912, the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927 and the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, but on neither of those occasions was this legislation consolidated. This means that those who are interested in the legislation respecting the harbour of Winnipeg and St. Boniface have to delve into the statute books of three different years, 1912, 1938 and 1955.
As I have said before, it is not a matter of world-shaking importance that these statutes be put in one place, but it does seem to be a matter of logic and common sense, and certainly it is a matter of convenience for those who have occasion to refer to this basic charter or constitution providing for the operations of this board.
As I have indicated on other occasions, the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commission is a body with a good deal of work to which it must attend. The harbour of Winnipeg and St. Boniface does not compare with some of the other harbours in Canada, but as I indicated by giving figures on March 17 there is a fair amount of shipping at the Alexander avenue wharf in this harbour, which happens to be located in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre.
I might also point out that the members of this board have been quite busy during the past 12 months. There has come before them a number of applications for the laying of pipe lines under both the Red and the Assiniboine rivers. In some cases the pipe lines have been for gas, in some cases for oil, in some cases for telephone trunk lines and in some cases for water distribution.
They have also had to deal with the preparations for the building of the mid-town bridge which crosses the Assiniboine river at the foot of Donald street, connecting the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) with the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor). The board has also had something to do with the borings in connection with the preliminary tests at the site of the proposed Disraeli bridge which is to cross the Red river in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre.
I indicate these activities merely to point out that this legislation is not the dead letter that it seems to be considered when it is left
3312	HOUSE OF
Winnipeg and St. Boniface Harbour as a statute of 1912, the amendments to which can be found only by searching the statutes of 1938 and 1955. It is for that reason that it seems to me to be a matter of convenience, logic and fairness to those concerned to have this legislation put into the one place.
As hon. members would expect, I have had some advice in connection with the preparation of this bill. The legal advice I have had is that this is the way to put all this legislation in one place and have it as a statute with legal effect. One can do this sort of thing by having the department print what is known as an office consolidation, but as everyone knows an office consolidation does not have the legal standing which is accorded to a statute passed by parliament.
On previous occasions when I have suggested that this be done it has been argued from the government side that it should not be considered for various reasons. It has been suggested that if it is done for this particular legislation it will have to be done for other legislation. I do not see that that is a very strong argument. It was contended also that it would be perfectly satisfactory to leave it the way it was. I admit readily that there would be no substantial loss if the legislation were left in the three places where it now is, but it seems to me that for the sake of tidying up things, for the sake of convenience, and as recognition of a good job which the members of this board do in the Winnipeg area-and they do it on a voluntary basis-the house might consent to the passing of this bill.
In conclusion I emphasize, as I did at the first, that it does not change anything. It just takes the three statutes to which I have referred and puts them together in a consolidated form, so that the legislation respecting the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commissioners might be found all in one place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no quarrel with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the sponsor of this bill, concerning that part of his remarks dealing with the historical background of the statutory provisions concerning the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commission. I wish also to state that his interest and the interest of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau), who also discussed this bill with me, in the activities of this harbour commission are very much appreciated by our department.
However, without going into a detailed study of the various sections of this bill, I wish to point out some of its effects. As hon. members know, the bill creates a new commission, and the existing corporation consequently disappears without providing for


maintaining the continuity of the present corporation. On the other hand, the existing act describes the harbour of Winnipeg and St. Boniface as comprising in part all the waters within the limits of the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface as they existed at the time of the passing of the original act, that is on 1st April, 1912. The present bill describes the harbour as comprising all the waters within the limits of the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface at the time of its passing, and this might have the effect of increasing or decreasing the limits of the present harbour, according to changes which might have taken place in the limits of both these cities since 1912.
Under the original act the harbour includes also such municipalities as were brought within the provisions of the act under section 4 as amended in 1938. These words are repeated in the present bill, but the effect is that the harbour would not indeed include the municipalities that were brought within the provisions of the present act. I wish also to add that the bill provides for the appointment of commissioners and that if the present act is repealed, the question arises whether or not the existing commissioners have ceased to hold office and whether also there must be new appointments. As hon. members know, it is customary in consolidating a statute of this kind to insert a transitional provision to ensure continuity of office but, of course, not beyond the terms of the existing tenures. The same remarks apply with respect to harbourmasters and other staff.
The present act also provides for the payment of the surplus profits to municipalities that have been brought under the provisions of the act as amended in 1938. As I have previously indicated, the present act includes all municipalities brought in under section 4 and, I repeat, as amended in 1938. The effect of repealing section 4 of the present act and replacing it, as the sponsor of this bill does, by an identical wording in the new bill would be to deprive of their share of the profits the municipalities brought in under the old act.
Furthermore, a similar problem arises in connection with clause 16 of the present act, dealing with the inspection of the books of the corporation by the audit departments of the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface and other municipalities brought in under the existing provisions; that is section 4 of the act.
Furthermore, I am informed by the drafting experts of the Department of Justice that the bill does not conform in all respects to the practices, as to language, form, and punctuation, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. I am further advised that if the consolidation is made it would be desirable

to make it uniform with the revised statutes. It is to be noted that it is not the intention of the sponsor of this bill, as he admitted a moment ago in speaking on second reading, to make any change in the existing statutory provisions, and therefore this is a private measure promoted as a matter of convenience only. For this reason the bill might be considered to be superfluous.
Mr. Speaker, in the circumstances, though I recognize that a consolidation might be desirable, I regret that I have to oppose the measure.

If one would read the words pronounced in this house in 1912 and in 1938-mostly in 1912-when an application was made to this house for the establishment of the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commission, one would find that the trade on the Red river was from two points in the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface alone.
Later on, in the amendment which was introduced here in 1938, it was requested that the new municipalities contiguous to both cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface but lying along the Red river could on application elect a representative to this commission. But if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had read carefully the bill asking for the formation of a Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commission he would have noticed that the amendment of 1938 would include the municipalities contiguous to the city of Winnipeg or the city of St. Boniface, whose limits were lying along the Red river.
There is a contradiction there between the two sections because, after all, the powers of the commission cover all waters within both cities. That takes in the Assiniboine river, the Seine river and, of course, the Red river which, at the time of the introduction of the bill in 1912, was the main trading route from the United States of America up to lake Winnipeg. The amendment of 1938 refers to all municipalities contiguous to the city of Winnipeg or the city of St. Boniface. They

There is on the statute books of the United Kingdom what is known as the consolidation of enactments (procedure) act, 1949, which is chapter 33 of the statutes of 1949. If those two gentlemen are satisfied that a bill which has been introduced as a consolidating bill does only that, just consolidates and does not make any changes, then there is a streamlined procedure by which the bill, after notice has been posted in the London Gazette for a required length of time, is referred to a committee without debate. I am not arguing anything that could be called partisan in any sense at all. I am just suggesting something that could result in tidying up our bits of legislation so they would be easier to find. At five o'clock I had commenced to make a few remarks about the treatment which was being given to newly born Canadian children whose parents as immigrants were denied family allowance benefits during their first year of residence in Canada. I know this is a sensitive point with many hundreds of thousands of new immigrants in our country. It must be remembered by the committee that these same people are future Canadian citizens. When we remember that as soon as an immigrant arrives in our country he becomes a taxpayer, and when we consider that during his first months and years in Canada every single cent counts in becoming properly established, I believe it will be agreed that this matter deserves some consideration by the minister and by the committee.
As I understand it, the situation which exists at present is rather unfair and unrealistic. At the present time the legal status of a child born in Canada, irrespective of the citizenship of its parents, is that such a child is a Canadian by birth. However, during the first year of residence of the child's parents in Canada such a Canadian child is denied the benefits which parliament provided in the matter of family allowances. If this interpretation is correct, and if the situation is as I understand it, it is rather paradoxical. On the one hand we have such a child born to newly arrived immigrants looked upon in the eyes of the law as a Canadian by birth; on the other hand that child is denied the benefits provided by the family allowance legislation during the first year of residence.
I was just wondering about the fairness of the situation. I would certainly appreciate it if the minister would explain the problem. I know that if we were able to eliminate that situation it would certainly be conducive to better relations between new arrivals in
3318	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration our country and Canadians. I touch briefly on this subject because I believe it is important. The situation should be remedied and I believe it will help to preserve happy relations among all segments of our Canadian society. I also believe it will show the new arrivals that we are concerned and would like to have them properly established when they arrive in Canada.
In conclusion, I should just like to take this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for the splendid co-operation he has given to me on several occasions, and that statement also applies to the various officials in his department.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to avail myself of this debate on the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to call the attention of the minister (Mr. Pickersgill) to a matter which worries me greatly at present, namely the matter of education at Pointe Bleue in the constituency I have the honour of representing in this house.
The Indian reserve at Pointe Bleue dates back about a hundred years. Today it has a population of some 1,125 people, making up 200 families, of which 110 are sedentary residents and 90 are nomads. In the reserve there are at present 272 children of school age; 110 attending the local Indian school, 28 the residential school at Fort George, while


5 go to other Indian schools, 55 attend provincial schools and 74 are not going to school at all.
The matter which I would like to bring to the attention of the department, has to do with nomad Indians. As those Indian families leave for the hunt in the fall and return only the following spring, some 100 Indian children of school age cannot attend school and therefore receive no education whatever.
Now the Indians of Pointe Bleue are becoming more and more sedentary. Besides, the majority of them are now in that category. However, children whose parents go out into the woods during the hunting season are deprived of the education to which they are entitled.
It is not a matter of preventing parents from taking their children with them when they go out hunting, but of encouraging them to let their children attend school in the reserve. I see only one way of doing it. As a matter of fact, after investigating the situation on the spot at the beginning of last month, together with the Pointe Bleue authorities, I have come to the conclusion that a residential school large enough to accommodate 120 pupils would be the only adequate solution to this problem, now or in the future. Since our Indians are ever desirous of living normally, they should be given that opportunity and should be provided for that purpose with every possible means of acquiring the education they need to earn a living.
If these children were placed in residential boarding schools while their parents are away hunting during the winter, they would receive a normal education which would enable them to face up successfully to the problem of earning their living. Indians, like all of us, are entitled to a better future.
If I am defending their interests here, it is because I know that these children of school age, being sent in this way to a residential institution would enjoy normal schooling, in every way comparable to that of the children of sedentary families who attend the local day schools. My attention has always been drawn to the fact that the problems affecting the Indians are often the result of deeds done by white people who took advantage of special circumstances to teach them ways of life which are foreign to them.
I urge the minister to consider my request with all the attention it deserves and to try to solve the problem by 1956 at the latest.
Building a residential school or boarding school for the children of wandering Indian families at Pointe Bleue would constitute an adequate solution.

Having said that, I come to the other matters that were being- discussed this afternoon, that is the regulations and the application of those regulations by the department.


I think, however much the minister may endeavour to explain them away, the regulations are unjustifiable in their present form. They are interpreted according to the whim and caprice of the individual official. They bring about in consequence a denial of fundamental rights. They constitute in fact arbitrary lawlessness.
What we in the opposition are endeavouring to prove is this, and for some reason the minister stands firm against any such argument, that the regulations should be reasonably interpreted in a straightforward and uniform manner, that the regulations should not be in the custody of the individual officials to interpret in accordance with their whim or prejudice or bias or for any other improper reason; that these are the regulations upon which human rights are determined.
The court of appeal of Ontario has very definitely stated, in the case to which the hon. member for Kamloops made extended reference this afternoon, that these regulations are unfair and unjust in the manner in which they are applied and were applied in the particular case. Why should it be necessary under those circumstances to press the minister for just one admission on his part that where there is wrongdoing-and there is always wrongdoing when the arbitrary will of an individual can place itself above the law-where such a condition of affairs applies, it will be his aim to remove the discrimination that is now inherent in this legislation and ensure that there shall be equality and justice to every individual according to law.
My hon. friend says he is not satisfied with the judgment of a recent appointee of this government, Mr. Justice Wilson; that he is not satisfied when that judgment is unanimously approved by the court of appeal, on which there were two judges already named by my hon. friend the member for Kamloops, and as well a former minister in charge of immigration, who found those regulations unjustly and tyrannically applied in the case in question. Why does the minister, instead of relying on those principles which ordinarily should actuate him in removing injustice, contend that he wants to carry the case forward because he is not satisfied with the unanimous decision on appeal?
Certainly it is a serious situation, it is a shocking situation, when a department of government is found so derelict in the application of the law as it was in the case in question. The minister should have stood up and said, "Well, after all we cannot expect perfection. There was wrongdoing in this case, as found by the courts of the country and we are going to remove anything in the nature of an injustice". That should be the

attitude of a department whose purpose should be the equal administration of law, and justice and the fair application of the rules to everybody. But for some reason this department is becoming entangled in administrative red tape, in some cases administered -and I mention this after consideration-by sawdust Caesars who believe they are above the law.

speechtext: A sawdust Caesar.

Some men, when they secure positions, must necessarily grow into those positions. Woodrow Wilson once said, "A man with responsibility either grows or swells." Some of these officials have not been growing, and they have not grown since the judgments of these various courts have been given, judgments that point out unfairness, tyranny and autocratic superiority on the part of officials; judgments that have indicated that the position in the department of immigration is that we have officials making the regulations, policing the regulations, interpreting the regulations and enforcing the regulations.
It is because of that fact, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Kamloops has pressed so often for a restoration of those principles that British justice has shown through the generations are necessary for the preservation of the fundamental freedoms of the individual. After all, there are only two ways in which freedom can be maintained. One is through parliament, the supreme court, the superior court, the highest court of the realm. That is where an appeal is being made now to the man who represents this department, to restore to it those things which it -has found throughout the generations must be maintained if the rights of the individual are to be assured. The other is through the courts.
While, in the course of the administration of the department, the courts have been bypassed in many cases, where the courts have spoken the department has not been game enough to accept the decisions of the courts and has endeavoured to carry on and on from court to court. Why not remove the reasons for injustices that were set out by the Hon. Mr. Justice Aylesworth and those associated with him in the Ontario court of appeal? Why not remove those wrongs, those injustices, rather than deny their existence and appeal against the decision? If the Supreme Court of Canada should ever have the opportunity of dealing with that case and confirms the judgment, does the department then intend to pass an order in council to ratify what was illegally done?

That was done before in the department of immigration and, Mr. Chairman, nothing better indicates stubborn truculence and autocratic lawlessness than the attitude of some departmental officials who, having lost in the courts, raise their decisions to a level above the courts by the passage of an order in council to legalize the unlawful. I do not say that in the course of administration of a department as large as the department of immigration small injustices will not arise from time to time. Human nature being what it is, they are bound to arise. But, sir, when a department has as its cornerstone the concept that where it is wrong it denies it, and where the courts find it is wrong it places itself above the courts by order in council, then indeed have you enthroned injustice; then indeed parliament has a right to speak.
I do ask the minister to reconsider what he said this afternoon, to decide that certain general principles are going to apply and that justice is going to be done as far as lies within the power of the minister. Fiat justitia. Let justice be done. That is all we ask from the minister. Let him accept such suggestions in the spirit in which they are given. Let him give the assurance that the department will bring into Canada by selective immigration those entitled to come here; and so that those in Canada will not be subject to deportation outside the law by the ipse dixit of some official who is above the law, we ask that the individual should be made acquainted with the charges against him. I do not suggest that he be given the names of the informants, but he should have placed before him the charges upon which the department believes he is not entitled to be considered a good Canadian citizen, in order that he may be able to answer those charges.
If that is not done, are we going back to the days of the star chamber where appointees of the crown sat, made their decisions and placed themselves above the law? That is my main criticism of the department of immigration today. I do not lay the slightest personal wrongdoing at the feet of the minister. But I do say that the minister, having inherited the department and having had seven or eight months to clear away these wrongs- and they are wrongs-we have a right to ask today, "What have you done? Why have you not acted? What is the reason that equity and law have been pushed aside and the arbitrary say-so of an individual in a department has been placed above the law of the land?"

I think, sir, erf what Lord Chesterfield said 125 years ago, so applicable to what is happening today in the department of unmigration. These are his words:
Let us consider that arbitary power has seldom or never been introduced into any country at once. It must be introduced by slow degrees, and, as it were, step by step lest the people should see its approach. The barriers and fences of the people's liberty must be plucked one by one, and some plausible pretence must be found for removing or hoodwinking, one after another, those sentries who are posted by the constitution of a free country for warning the people of their danger.
What are the sentries? The sentries are the rule of law, equity under the law, the right of an individual not to be convicted in his absence, the right of a person charged to know the nature of the charge against him. Remove these safeguards, destroy these sentries and, Mr. Chairman, every country's history tells its story. This is as true today as it was 175 years ago when Lord Acton said: "All power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."

I shall try to take the points the hon. gentleman raised in opposite order to the order in which he raised them. He said this department had overruled the courts

by order in council. I am only a simple layman and the hon. gentleman is a learned member of the bar, but I do not know of any court in this country in which an order in council could override the law or would be regarded for one instant as having any such effect.
What happened in the case to which he has alluded is this. The governor in council made certain regulations which he believed meant something. The Supreme Court of Canada said they meant something else. The governor in council who, in the first place, had the power to make these regulations then amended the regulations to make them mean what he thought they had meant in the first place. There was nothing retroactive about that change at all.
The hon. gentleman said the department by-passed the courts. At the same time he objected to my statement that we were going to appeal to the supreme court. Well, it is an odd kind of by-passing, sir, to appeal to the supreme court. I did not say I was satisfied or dissatisfied with the decision of the court of appeal of Ontario. I said the decision of the court of appeal was so important from the point of view of law that I felt it was essential for the administration of this department to know from the final arbiter, which is the supreme court, what the law really was. That is the reason, and the sole reason, I intend to recommend to my hon. friend the Attorney General of Canada that this case be appealed.
Now, it is of course totally untrue-I am not accusing the hon. gentleman-it is totally inaccurate to say that the Immigration Act is administered according to the whim and caprice of government officials. It is nothing of the kind. The regulations are made just as clearly and precisely as it is possible to make regulations which must apply to the almost infinite variety of human beings with whom the department has to deal. I do not know of any possible way in which regulations could be drafted that would create the kind of sure guide needed for every conceivable situation that might arise when some three or four million applications for admission to this country were being considered. This illustrates the magnitude of the problem with which the immigration branch has had to deal in the last 10 years. In order to get
1,200,000	immigrants it must have meant that at some stage or other there were three or four times that many people making approaches to our offices.

In the case of an application for admission there is nothing in the Immigration Act, which the hon. member for Prince Albert helped to put on the statute books and with which I had nothing to do because I was not a member of parliament at that time, which gives any person except a citizen of Canada residing outside of Canada the right to enter this country. And I must say that anything complimentary that is said about me or my administration-and in passing I would thank the hon. member for the rather kind things he did say-should be multiplied many times over in reference to my predecessor. I have said before in the house, and I wish to say again, that if at the end of four years I can believe that I have administered this department anything like as well as my predecessor did, I will be quite satisfied that I have served the Canadian people well.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I know I am rather given to talking too much, and I sometimes have to pay a certain penalty for it. Oh, it is not always amusing; but when something silly happens, then I try to regard it as silly. I think perhaps this country would be better off if more of us did that.
The hon. member for Prince Albert talked about the whim and caprice of individual officials. Since I became minister of the [DOT]department, even at times when some people seemed to think I was enjoying myself at the expense of the taxpayers, I have made an effort to visit the offices of this department in every place I have ever been; and I say without fear of successful, detailed contradiction that, taken by and large, the officials of this department are hard-working and conscientious and that they try, sometimes I think almost too hard, to adhere literally to the regulations.
I admit there have been a few officials who have not been satisfactory, and that one or two of them have had to be prosecuted in the courts. I hope I shall never lack the courage, if I find there is any wrongdoing anywhere in my department, to deal with it, and to deal with it regardless of what the consequences may be for me or for anybody else. If I do any wrong, then I shall endeavour to the best of my ability to undo it. I know it is impossible to deal with the number of people that this department has to deal with in a year, during which there are 50 million border crossings, and not make mistakes; and of course there are mistakes made. But what surprises me is that there are so few.
I think that is really all I have to say in reply to the hon. member for Prince Albert.

Mr. Chairman, I was pleasantly surprised a moment ago when, for the first time-and that does not mean that he has not done so previously-I heard the minister (Mr. Pickersgill) reply to the hon.


member for Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve) in excellent French, for which I congratulate him. He certainly has the admiration of all those present in the house. I believe we should congratulate him on his magnificent effort.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, convinced as I am that he will readily understand the few remarks I wish to make, I do not hesitate to speak in my mother tongue, thereby confirming the fact that there are two official languages in our country.
Although I have just congratulated the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for his generous gesture, I nonetheless wish to take him to task for certain statements he made recently, although I do not intend to repeat the ones which have been mentioned here in this house. I would like to refer, if you wish, to the same speech he made at Victoria and which contained a remark to which attention has not yet been called.
I find it in Le Soleil of Quebec, a newspaper which is the organ of the party now in power in the country. It is a dispatch from the Canadian Press, dated April 12, 1955, and entitled:
The immigrant who is willing to work will find employment.
This statement is followed by the name (Pickersgill), in brackets, meaning that those remarks were uttered by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. According to that statement-and I am quoting what is between quotation marks, which means, I believe, that those are the exact words of the minister-
It is not difficult to settle in Canada, in spite of growing unemployment, provided an average worker does not hesitate to accept any kind of employment.
Reference was made a moment ago to the irresponsible statements which the minister makes on a great many occasions. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that no statement could have been more irresponsible than those remarks made by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in his speech in Victoria. By contending that an immigrant coming to this country who truly wishes to work can find employment, the minister has insulted the
700,000	Canadian workers who are now unemployed, because his statement amounts to denying that 700,000 Canadian workers have decided to find employment. That is perfectly ridiculous and I repeat it is a serious insult to the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, the dispatch goes on to say -hon. members on the other side find that

funny, Mr. Chairman, but we on this side respect our opinions and we are not afraid to rise and defend the rights of Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I continue with the article:
Such was the opinion expressed yesterday by the federal Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in answer to the charges made that he had allowed immigrants into the country in spite of the fact that a large number of Canadians are at present out of work.
Further on in the same article there is a quotation from the minister. I will return to this question later.
For the moment let us say that the minister, in the same speech, admitted that unemployment had reached a very high level in this country. According to the statement made by him this very afternoon, Canada has received, since the end of the last war,
1,200,000	immigrants. Whatever may be said to the contrary, this massive immigration policy implemented by the Canadian government since the last world war is no doubt one of the reasons, if not the only reason, why we are at this time faced with such heavy unemployment. The reason is evident and I do not blame the minister since it is only very recently that he took over the portfolio of that department.
What is the economic contribution of the immigrants? On one hand, a few small industries, bringing with them some capital, have been established here and there in Canada. At the same time, a certain number of craftsmen have brought us new techniques and modern methods. On the other hand, it must be admitted that the large majority of the newcomers for the past ten years have been industrial or unskilled workers. To support that statement I think it is sufficient to bring forward the following statistics: 13 per cent only of the total number of newcomers have
29, 1955	3325
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration established themselves on farms, while 5 per cent only went to work as domestic help, notwithstanding the fact that most of the immigrants claimed to belong to these categories in order to gain admission into Canada. Shortly after they were through with that work, either as farm-hands or as servants, these people made their way to our large centres, and we cannot blame them for being attracted by good salaries and for wanting to be able to meet fellow countrymen.
However, hundreds of thousands of these people have increased our industrial labour force, which means that they had to find some 200,000 homes in our industrial centres where the housing problem was already acute. Most of them work for large corporations which get fabulous government contracts, such as Canadair, in Montreal, Canadian Vickers and a number of crown corporations. But what, to my mind, is outrageous is that the moment there is some unemployment the first ones to be laid off are the native sons of Canada, while the newcomers are kept on the job.
I do not want to cast reflection on people who left their country to take refuge in Canada, where they can at least find peace and freedom. I would be the last one to blame them for trying to become Canadian citizens when they wanted to flee from communism and slavery. But I consider that we have not shown good sense in our immigration policy.
I feel that not enough thought was given to this matter and that, in particular, we did not take economic conditions in Canada into consideration before increasing our population to a considerable extent. Lest I be misunderstood let me say that I am not opposed to immigration. On the contrary, I am in favour of selective well-chosen immigration-

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Well, that is what we have now.

But immigration should only be favoured when this country is prosperous, when everyone has a job. Immigration must be on a selective basis, as I said a moment ago, and provided only that we enjoy here in Canada a certain measure of economic stability.
As for those whom we have welcomed -most are now Canadian citizens perhaps-* let us hope that they will find in Canada what they really came here for so that some day they may be Canadians worthy of the name.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Let us rather combine our efforts, so as to keep our own people in this country and prevent thousands of Canadians who are unable to find any work in Canada from emigrating to the United States.
Following these remarks, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if Canada is in a position to continue to receive immigrants this year, and in the future, at the same rate as it has since the end of the war.
I would also like to say a word about the racial distribution of our people with regard to immigration. Since the end of the war Anglo-Canadians, representing a little less than 50 per cent of our population, have received reinforcements out of the 1,200,000 odd new Canadians arriving here, to the extent of 30 per cent. French-speaking Canadians, who make up 30 per cent of our people, have only received reinforcements to the extent of 2 per cent.
I will not blame my English-speaking fellow citizens for requiring even more reinforcements, for asking that more Englishspeaking people be admitted to this country. But, as a French-speaking Canadian, as a citizen of Quebec, I think that because of their contribution to Canada since confederation, French Canadians deserve a greater proportion so as to stabilize Our group better within the Canadian nation.
I would therefore ask the hon. minister, first, for a temporary halt on further landings of immigrants in this country, until the day when our economic balance is restored and every Canadian has his own job enabling him to face his obligations, to maintain his family, and to be, at the same time, a true Canadian.
Mr. Chairman, may I very sincerely congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Holowach), who just now touched upon a most important and serious point. I agree with the hon. member who said that it is inconceivable that a child born in Canada, even on the day after the arrival of its parents in this country, should be denied the family allowance to which it is entitled. Being born in Canada, the child is a Canadian citizen and, once a Canadian citizen, comes under Canadian law.

Mr. Chairman, before we come to the details of the items, I should like to make one or two general observations arising partly out of what the minister has said. Perhaps it would not be out of place to say something about the proceedings of the special committee on estimates. It seems to me that the committee has accomplished a fair part of the work of this committee of supply in reviewing many of the details of the administration of the department. That is perhaps evidenced by what has been said so far, because our discussion today has not been on the details of administration but on one or two general matters which have occupied the committee up to this time.
I think it proper to say that, as a member of that committee, I find no room for complaint about the conduct of the officials of the department whom we had the privilege of examining, the deputy minister and those who were with him. We were free to ask them questions directly, and we received our answers in many cases directly. Sometimes the minister assumed that a matter of policy was involved and undertook to speak for his officials, but by and large we received the information which we asked for and were not refused information. I think perhaps that, rather than putting it on a negative basis and saying that we have no complaints,
I should say that the procedure of the

special committee commends itself to me as a distinct improvement over what can. be done in this committee of supply.
I will not go as far as that with respect to the minister himself. We complained about his being a member of the committee at the same time as he was a witness appearing before the committee to answer for his department, but that matter was resolved by force majeure. We were not able to carry our point. We had the minister speaking on both sides of the issue and we also had him as a witness. I must say that if you review the transcript you will find that the minister used as much of the time of the committee as almost anyone else.
