To my mind what was involved was not the production before the committee of some mysterious documents. It seems to me that the discussion of those documents was used as a screen to obscure the fact that here was a witness who might have given information to the committee out of his own experience, but whose evidence was refused by the committee. I say that because Mr. Taylor, as the minister himself said, is a practising lawyer having a good deal of immigration work, who undertook to review some 200 cases which had come before the department.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
I should like to make it clear, if I did not this afternoon, that the
3329
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration 200 cases were 200 cases that came to Mr. Taylor in his law practice.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
I am not denying they were 200 cases that came to him in his law practice. He probably knew them better than if information about them had come to him by hearsay. But whatever they were, whether they were cases of his clients or partly of his clients and partly of clients of other lawyers in any event he reviewed the cases and he had opinions, as a result of that experience, as to the administration of the department. It seems to me that his opinions based on that experience were the sort of evidence that might have been useful to a committee which was reviewing the administration of the department. He had made criticisms and had offered his evidence. If there was nothing to his criticisms, surely it would have been better for the department and the minister to allow the witness to come, say what he had to say, and if his complaints could be met, meet them and dispose of them.
The minister has made quite a play of meeting all issues head-on, and I must say that in his own conduct in respect of other things he appears to do that. He does not balk at any questions, nor does he refuse any issue. However, in this particular case this man offered his evidence and the minister, instead of allowing his evidence to be heard, which could have been done without inconvenience to the committee or to the witness, hid behind the substantial majority of government members on the committee, and on three or four occasions when the question was brought to a head he permitted the vote of the government majority to settle the question of whether this man should appear.
The only consequence is that the suspicion arising out of such criticisms as this man made, and which we have all heard to some extent, lingers instead of being met. If there is any grievance it has not been remedied. If there was no grievance the suspicion continues, to the discredit and discomfort of the minister. Therefore I suggest that in that particular instance, when there was no question of producing documents but simply of allowing a man who had special experience to come and tell his story and be examined before a committee, it was wrong for the government majority to refuse by sheer weight of numbers to hear that evidence, and it was wrong for the minister to countenance that action.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a general complaint with regard to the arbitrary manner in which a great deal of the immigration work of the department seems to be
3330	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration carried on, and the fact that the department seems to be very stiff-necked about its own errors and extremely difficult to persuade to change any decision that has been made, no matter how wrong it may be shown to have been in the first place. In this connection I should like to cite the case of a woman, Mrs. Jessie Wilson, who came to this country from Australia.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit one very brief interruption? If we are now going to have immigration, can we carry item 59 and go on with immigration, because it would be a great help to me to have the director here?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: What I have to say is by way of general criticism of the departmental administration and the way things are carried on. I think this is probably the proper place to bring up the matter, rather than attempt to bring it up in detail at another time when I might be told it was not really properly applicable at that point.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Strictly speaking it is not properly applicable on the item of departmental administration. It is properly applicable on the immigration branch item. However, I am not insisting on the point at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: I am not going to rule the hon. member for Calgary North out of order. I am not suggesting it is the most efficient method, but it has been the practice to allow almost any discussion relevant to the department on the first item. It will be up to hon. members who wish to raise these points whether they insist on raising them at this stage or whether it would suit their purposes better to do so when the appropriate officials are before the minister.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I think this particular case illustrates quite well the arbitrary methods frequently used, I am afraid, in the immigration department, and the impossibility almost of getting the department, including the minister in charge, to rectify anything, make any change or admit that any error has taken place. I took up this case first of all with the present Minister of Finance when he was minister of citizenship and immigration. I thought I was making some progress on it, but nothing happened. I took it up with the present minister, and still nothing happened.
Briefly, the circumstances in the case were these. This woman, Mrs. Jessie Wilson, had a son living in Calgary. He had been an air trainee during the war, married a Canadian girl, came back and settled there and is living there at the present time. His mother came over to visit him. Before she left Australia


she took the usual physical examination. As a matter of fact she bought a return passage. She was not sure whether she wanted to settle here and live in Canada, as her son was urging her to do, or whether she would go back. In any event, she took the usual medical examination and it was discovered by X-ray that she had a tubercular scar of some sort on her lung. The people in Australia told her the scar was of old origin, was not active, and that for all practical purposes she was quite fit and well.
Mrs. Wilson landed in Vancouver and was allowed to remain 24 hours, when she was put on a ship and sent back to Australia. The main points of the story are perhaps best set out in an editorial in the Calgary Herald, which took up this case. I shall read briefly from this editorial which is headed, "What's Happening in Immigration?"
We do not like the sound of the reports of episodes which keep trickling out of the machinery of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
The latest of these concerns Mrs. Jessie Alice Wilson, an Australian woman, who after travelling all the way to Canada to visit her son in Calgary was summarily sent home by the immigration authorities in Vancouver. The authorities denied entry to Mrs. Wilson on the grounds that she was suffering from tuberculosis, and they took this decision despite a recommendation from some Vancouver doctors who examined her that "it would not be advisable to order deportation until conclusive tests had been made."
As a matter of fact, I have here a photostatic copy of a letter which was given to Mrs. Wilson in Vancouver when she was examined there.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Examined by whom?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
I am just beginning to read it. This letter is headed, "Division of tuberculosis control, department of health and welfare, Willow chest centre, Vancouver, B.C.; January 19, 1954". It is addressed to the department of immigration, Vancouver, B.C.; re Mrs. Jessie Alice Wilson. It reads as follows:
Chest X-ray of January 18, 1954, reveals fibrotie appearing infiltration in the peripheral portion of the first and second right interspaces. There would appear to be a calcification deposited in these areas. This has the appearance of an arrested area of tuberculosis and it is our opinion that it would not be justifiable to deport this patient on the strength of the present findings.
Before a dogmatic opinion regarding this area can be given, further followup studies by X-ray and stomach washings would be necessary.
Yours truly,
Signed "D. Mowat"
D. Mowat, M.D.,
Clinic director.
Willow chest centre.
What happened was that this woman was examined by an immigration doctor and he said she had pulmonary tuberculosis. She

had been told before she left Australia that she did not, that this was just an old scar. She was examined by this man who is head of the provincial tuberculosis centre in British Columbia, and he advised that she should not be deported on the strength of anything he could find. In spite of that she was deported. Complaints were made, and I took the matter up with the present' Minister of Finance, who said he would have the case reviewed. He did have it reviewed, but the doctors in the immigration department said, "No; pulmonary tuberculosis. We cannot have the woman in here".

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
I must rise on a point of
order. The hon. gentleman is not talking about matters over which I, as minister, or my predecessor, as minister, had any control whatever. The determination of these cases, as I understand it, is carried out for us by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do not attempt to substitute my judgment for the official medical advice that I receive from the proper, competent people. I have not the right under the law to substitute myself, nor have any of the officials of this department, for that matter. Therefore if the hon. gentleman wishes to raise these individual cases, and to complain about the checking of another department of government, it does not seem to me quite reasonable-

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Don't try to worm out of it.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: -that the time allotted for this department should be taken up with it.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
The examination of people wishing to enter this country is performed, as the minister has just said, on behalf of the department of immigration by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The doctors who perform that examination technically belong to the Department of National Health and Welfare, but the work is done for the department of immigration. It is the immigration people who act on whatever the findings are.
As I said at the beginning, I brought this case up for the purpose of showing the arbitrary methods that are followed by the department and the subsequent impossibility, when a mistake has been discovered, to get the immigration people to admit it. In view of the medical evidence, some of which I have given here, I do not think there is any doubt that this woman never should have been deported. I have two full sheets containing clinical observations by tuberculosis specialists in Australia, both before she came to this country and after she went back. All the observations are to the effect she has 50433-211J
29, 1955	3331
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration no active tuberculosis. She has an old scar, just as many people have, and to all intents and purposes she is a fit woman.
In spite of this medical evidence, this doctor working for the department of immigration made a mistake. I do not think there is any doubt about it. He diagnosed this woman as having pulmonary tuberculosis, yet all the tuberculosis experts who have examined her claim she does not have pulmonary tuberculosis. On the basis of this diagnosis the woman was allowed to stay in the country only 24 hours. The department paid no attention to the report of the tuberculosis specialists to whom they took the woman during the brief time she was here. She was sent back to Australia, and furthermore she has not been allowed to return here. Subsequent efforts on the part of her son to get her back to this country have all been turned down, still on the basis she has pulmonary tuberculosis.
What it boils down to, and I wrote the minister to this effect, is that it would appear that once a mistake has been made by one of the doctors advising this department, then the department refuses to admit that mistake. They insist he was right, no matter how much medical evidence you bring to show he was wrong. The department acts on that basis. I shall not take the time of the house to read all this medical evidence. I have two full pages of clinical reports from tuberculosis specialists, which are on the letterhead of the anti-tuberculosis association of New South Wales.
This case has dragged on now for a year and a quarter, but no matter what medical evidence you bring in the answer is always the same, that the woman has pulmonary tuberculosis. The department maintains this position in spite of the fact that every tuberculosis specialist, both in Canada and in Australia, who has examined her says she has not and never did have it. The woman was shipped back in this arbitrary manner at great expense which she could ill afford, and she has been refused entry since. If that is not an arbitrary method of carrying on immigration to this country then I do not know what you could call arbitrary treatment.
The son became a Canadian some years ago, and first arrived in this country as a trainee under the air scheme. Both ministers, one after the other, who have handled this department during this period refused to have anything done about the matter. In other words they took the attitude, "Well, our doctor-who I do not suppose for a minute was an expert on tuberculosis-"said she had pulmonary tuberculosis and so far as we are concerned that is it." They do not
3332	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration care what the Australian doctors say. They do not care what the Vancouver specialist says. So far as they are concerned she has pulmonary tuberculosis and they are not going to let her in.
It is this type of case that has caused a great deal of distrust of the department of immigration. It is this type of thing that has caused a large number of people to believe there is something particularly wrong, particularly rotten so far as the department of immigration is concerned. I am not saying that is the case. As a matter of fact I am quite sure that the department-

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: I am.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: -has many very able officials who do their best to carry on things in a reasonable way. This, however, indicated a stubborn attitude right at the top on the part of the minister who is now in charge, and the minister who was formerly in charge. When you have a minister in charge of a department who adopts an absolutely stubborn attitude of that sort, -and refuses to let reason enter into the settlement of any of these cases, then I do not think it is fair to blame the officials. I think the blame should be placed right squarely on the shoulders of the minister; and I think in this particular case the minister should give an undertaking to have a new review made immediately with a view to letting this woman come into this country to visit her son.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: I shall be delighted to review the case. I do not think I have ever refused any member of this house, including the hon. member who has just spoken, a review of any case I have been asked to review.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: And I might say in that connection that if the minister is going to review it in the same way he reviewed it before, merely reiterating the statement that the doctor examined her once on behalf of the department, and then say "Our people know best", it will not be enough. Just wait until I get this letter from my file and read what he said in connection with the medical evidence. I find on looking in my file that I do not have the letter I intended to read.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
Well, I have so many of these letters here that it is hard to find them in a minute. But the first letter was to the effect that the medical men in the employ of the department and working for the department knew better than any of the outside doctors


what the requirements for immigration purposes would be. Then after I did get a review of the matter the minister wrote saying this:
A medical report has now been received from the chief of the Department of National Health and Welfare, immigration service, concerning Mrs. Jessie Alice Wilson of Australia.
Dr. Reid states that Mrs. Wilson is certified under section 5, s.s. (b) of the Immigration Act, and that she will require an over-all period of observation of at least two years, before up-grading can be considered.
In other words, apparently all Dr. Reid did was take the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis and say, "We cannot look at her for two years, until it has a chance to clear up". On the other hand all the experts in this line who examined the woman, who took sputum tests, who X-rayed her, and everything else, insisted that she never did have pulmonary tuberculosis, that all she had was a bit of a scar that had been there for years and did no harm at all.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: I think that was one of the worst exhibitions this House of Commons has ever seen, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, when his estimates were being discussed and when an item of his department was being drawn to the attention of the house, getting to his feet and declaring that because somebody else was trying to help to do the job he cannot do himself, it is not good enough because it is not in his department, that the doctors belong to another department. And in effect he says, "Therefore my time should not be wasted. You should not talk about my department, because my assistants who are trying to enable me to do the semblance of a decent job do not belong to my department." That is a fine attitude to take.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
He says they are not his
babies.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: No, they are not his babies. The majority of cabinet ministers in the Liberal government take the responsibility for everything that is done in those departments. But here we have a new minister trying to shove it off, on to another department. That is a fine manner in which to do business.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES

carry?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say a few words. I sat on the estimates committee when it dealt with the estimates of this department. It was emphasized on many occasions that the department had not been careful enough in screening immigrants

entering this country. We sat through hour after hour listening to that kind of criticism. It was opposition members sitting on that committee who made all the criticism. There was information the minister was unable to give them with respect to screening in Europe, and they were not satisfied with that. They wanted to have all the details.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES
speechtext: That is not-

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND ST. BONIFACE HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS CONSOLIDATION OF EXISTING STATUTES

You have had your say, Fergie; now I want mine. They wanted all the details about how the screening was done, to find out if the department was being careful enough. I have heard the accusation made on the floor of the house that immigrants who did come to this country were found to be in ill health, and we have been criticized for having to take care of them.
Tonight the shoe is on the other foot. I know Dr. Reid very well, and I have a lot of confidence in his judgment. But they say Dr. Reid knows nothing about this disease, and that the only thing we can do is discard any advice that might be at our disposal and take that of some other doctor who might be in British Columbia or Australia. I feel we have doctors of our own in this country who can take care of this situation. I do believe the screening that is being done for this department should not be condemned, and that we should support it.
